source_cards.front: Who may get Class M and Class MJ licenses, and how is a second class shown?
source_cards.back: Class M starts at eighteen, or seventeen with driver education, and Class MJ at sixteen, both for motorcycles and mopeds with junior limits on MJ; holding motorcycle plus another class prints both on one card such as Class DM.

source_cards.front: What can the Enhanced license be used for, and who may get one?
source_cards.back: The Enhanced license serves land and sea crossings with Canada, Mexico, Bermuda and the Caribbean as a passport substitute, works for domestic air travel, needs state residence plus United States citizenship, and also issues for commercial and motorcycle classes.

source_cards.front: What other manuals, languages and school pre-tests are available?
source_cards.back: Motorcycle applicants also study manual MV-21MC and commercial applicants manual CDL-ten for a separate test; Class D tests run multilingual on touch screens or paper; students from fifteen years eleven months may pre-test through OKTA at participating high schools in English or Spanish with instant on-screen scoring, and schools need no driver-ed program, just a connected computer, printer and monitor.

source_cards.front: What must the test car and the arriving driver bring, and how do you book?

source_cards.front: What passenger and supervision rules apply to permit and junior motorcycle and moped riders?
source_cards.back: Permit and junior motorcycle and moped riders carry no passenger but the supervisor, who holds the same-class license, stays within a quarter mile in general control, and should keep the rider visible.

source_cards.front: What passenger and supervision rules apply to a Class M or MJ motorcycle or moped learner permit or junior license?
source_cards.back: A Class M or MJ motorcycle or moped learner permit or junior license allows no passenger except a supervising driver licensed for the same class, who must maintain general supervision and control within one quarter mile and should ideally keep the rider in sight.

source_cards.front: What does a stop sign require, and where exactly do you stop?
source_cards.back: The red-and-white stop sign demands a full stop with right-of-way yielded, halting before the stop line, else the crosswalk, else the nearest point with a clear view into the intersection.

source_cards.front: What does a yield sign require?
source_cards.back: The red-and-white yield sign demands slowing, traffic checks and readiness to stop, a full stop whenever conditions require, and yielded right-of-way.

source_cards.front: How do stop and yield signs differ, and what stopping-point order applies at a stop sign?
source_cards.back: A stop sign requires a full stop every time before yielding right-of-way—stopping before the stop line, else the crosswalk, else the nearest point with a view of cross traffic—whereas a yield sign requires slowing down, checking traffic, yielding right-of-way, and stopping fully only when traffic conditions require it.

source_cards.front: How are signal lights arranged, and what do you do at a dead signal?
source_cards.back: Signals normally stack red, yellow and green top-to-bottom or left-to-right, appearing lone, flashing, round or arrowed, and dead or broken signals force a stop-sign stop followed by right-of-way rules unless an officer directs otherwise.

source_cards.front: What do a steady green light and a green arrow allow?
source_cards.back: Steady green and green arrows both permit movement while still yielding right-of-way as the law requires.

source_cards.front: When do stop lines and crosswalk lines require a stop?
source_cards.back: Signed or signaled intersections may paint a white stop line or parallel crosswalk lines, stopping falls before whichever exists only when a device, officer or yielding pedestrian, skater or scooter user demands it, and set-back single lines shelter truck turning room.

source_cards.front: What do a dead signal and a flashing red have in common?
source_cards.back: Dead signals degrade to stop-sign behavior with right-of-way rules, the same fallback a flashing red gives, while officers can override both.

source_cards.front: What does the Move Over law require?
source_cards.back: The Move Over law demands care, reduced speed and, on multilane parkways, interstates and controlled roads, a lane shift away from shoulder-stopped emergency and hazard vehicles flashing emergency, amber or blue-green lights unless unsafe, plus blue-green-light vehicles and any shoulder-parked vehicle on parkways and controlled highways, all punishable as a moving violation.
